doc.title: Johnny Varro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: The Honeymooners and Jackie Gleason shows
summary: Phil Napoleon's band played warm-ups for The Honeymooners, then Gleason's Miami show and train parties.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Tell me about “The Jackie Gleason Show” and how that came about.

Well when I was at Nick’s with Phil Napoleon in ’54, a lot of celebrities used to come in, people would come in and dig the music and stay until, God we went until four o’clock in the morning in those days. And we’d have an audience on for that last set, we’d have at least two dozen people there sitting around the bar waiting. I guess they had to go to work in the morning but the music was entrancing to them. And this one night Jackie came in with an entourage and sat and listened to the and loved the band. Phil Napoleon — I might have misled you in some way, I said it was kind of tight and two beat and all that, but it was really a very good band, very clean and some great players. Jackie loved that. He loved the music. So he was starting “The Honeymooners.” And he hired us as a unit to play for the warm-ups. Like we’d play a half hour before the show was to start as the people would come in and they’d sit in the audience and we’d play about a half hour. And then we’d take a break and the announcer would come out and explain what’s going to go on with the show and then we’d come up and we’d do another tune. And then the show was ready to start. And we would play between scene changes and play them off on the end. And they had the front row set for us so that when we finished playing we’d just sit down right there. And here we watched all those original Honeymooners being done live. I mean I see them and I hear us laughing. Phil Napoleon had a very infectious laugh. And every once in a while I’ll hear him and I’ll say oh God, there’s Phil. Maybe to score brownie points with Jackie, I don’t know, laughing harder than usual. I shouldn’t say that. But we did that for two years. So we caught all those Honeymooner things. I mean it was just classic stuff. And they’re so great. And that lasted for two years. And then several years later, let’s see that was ’55. Then in ’65 I got a call — I’m jumping again — but Jackie had the show in Miami, the “American Scene Magazine” I think it was called, an

hour variety show. And I got a call from Phil Napoleon again and he says, “What are you doing at this point?” I said, “Nothing.” He says, “Come on down, I’ve got the Gleason show, I’ve got the race track on Saturdays, and we’ve got a steady gig in the Roney Plaza Hotel six nights a week.” I said, “Send me a ticket.” And it was snowing, it was January, it was snowing in New York and horrible and freezing and I had no work. He says, “The temperature here is 78 degrees.” “Send me a ticket. I’ll be right down.” And I worked for the Gleason show for another two years on that. I had never worked directly for Gleason, but worked for Phil, Phil Napoleon. And we played all his parties, we played the train ride down, he used to have a train. It would start out with a party at Toots Shor’s in New York and we’d be transported to a train, Gleason had his own train, and we’d go down to Miami by train and play on the train and party it up. It was just one big party with all the June Taylor dancers and Art Carney and Frank Fontaine and all that whole bunch, Sheila McRae.
Oh, Frank Fontaine, I haven’t heard that name in a while. He was a great drunk, wasn’t he?
In watching those Honeymooner shows, did they ever have moments where things went wrong, or were you aware of them?

They rarely did two takes on something, unless something went drastically wrong then they might stop it and we’d get up and play, and they’d make some changes or reset themselves. But hardly ever. I remember one time in Miami after the original Honeymooners they did a thing and Jackie was supposed to crash into a brick wall. And he did, something happened and he went crashing into this wall and he broke either his wrist or his ankle I forget what it was. But he broke something, but he went on and carried out and finished the whole night and he wasn’t going to take a break for that. Yeah he was quite a guy.
